analysis.one_liner: Lets federally funded chip factories skip or shortcut environmental reviews.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, backed by 13 House members, died in committee without a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies building or expanding computer chip factories with federal money from the CHIPS Act would get big exemptions from the National Environmental Policy Act, the law that requires the government to study a project's environmental impact before approving it. For projects not fully exempt, the Commerce Department would take over the review from other agencies, rely on a single document, reuse old studies, and could hand the whole review to a state. It would also shorten the window for challenging these decisions in court to 150 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Chipmakers receiving federal CHIPS Act funding. Their plants could be built or expanded faster, with fewer environmental studies, fewer agency sign-offs, and a much shorter window for neighbors or conservation groups to challenge approvals in court.

how_it_helps.text: Exempts federally assisted semiconductor projects from environmental review under NEPA and the National Historic Preservation Act when the project has already started, stays on an existing site, uses a loan or loan guarantee, or gets less than 15 percent of its cost from federal grants [S2] [S3].

For projects that still need review, lets the Commerce Department act as lead agency, prepare one combined environmental document for all permits, and rely on prior studies rather than starting over [S2] [S3].

Lets the Commerce Secretary freely reuse any categorical exclusion another federal agency has adopted to skip review, and prevents those exclusions from being questioned for unusual circumstances [S3].
Gives states the option to take over the federal environmental review for chip projects, and bars most lawsuits over these approvals unless filed within 150 days of the announcement [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People living near proposed or expanding chip factories, and the public generally. They would lose the full environmental review process — water use, pollution, traffic, and historic site impacts would get less study — and would have only 150 days to sue over a flawed approval instead of the longer windows courts have recognized.

drawbacks.text: Exempting projects from NEPA review removes the public process that documents a plant's environmental impact and gives affected residents a formal way to raise concerns before construction [S3].

The Secretary could declare a state's environmental rules 'functionally equivalent' to federal law in his or her sole discretion, with no defined standard, and categorical exclusions would not be subject to the usual extraordinary-circumstances check [S3].
A 150-day deadline for legal challenges is short enough that community groups with limited resources could find out too late to mount a case [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Speeding up construction of chip factories has a real national goal behind it — securing the chip supply — and long federal reviews can delay projects that have already passed many local permits. But this bill goes further than coordination: it exempts whole categories of projects from environmental review entirely, concentrates authority in one agency, and closes the courthouse door quickly. The public loses transparency and legal recourse, and the savings in time are not guaranteed to be passed on to anyone but the companies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees when introduced, and two weeks later to a subcommittee, but no committee ever held a hearing or voted to send it to the floor, and the Congress ended with it still pending.

narrative.text: Rep. Jennifer Kiggans introduced the bill on July 11, 2023, joined by Reps. Peters (D-TX), Williams (R-NY), Allred (D-TX), and McCaul (R-TX) [S1] [S3].

It was referred to four committees — Science, Space, and Technology; Energy and Commerce; Armed Services; and Natural Resources — and on July 14, 2023 to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S5].
Twelve members cosponsored the bill, evenly split between 6 Republicans and 6 Democrats [S4].
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities near proposed chip plants keep the standard environmental review process and normal access to the courts, since the exemptions and the shortened 150-day lawsuit window never became law. Chipmakers receiving CHIPS funding remain subject to full federal review of their projects.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Residents who kept full environmental review rights

for.name: Rep. Jennifer Kiggans
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt and streamline environmental reviews for federally funded chip projects

for.name: Reps. Peters, Allred (D-TX), McCaul (R-TX), and Williams (R-NY)
for.what_they_did: Joined the sponsor at introduction, making the bill bipartisan from day one

for.name: 6 of 226 House Republicans and 6 of 216 House Democrats

against.name: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (with Energy and Commerce, Armed Services, and Natural Resources)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill never advanced; its subcommittee received the bill in July 2023 and took no further recorded action

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split — the Republican sponsor drew 6 Republican and 6 Democratic cosponsors — and no recorded opposition ever appeared, so the bill died of inaction rather than a partisan fight.

industries.note: CHIPS-funded chipmakers would get their factories built faster by skipping or compressing federal environmental review, with a shortened window for challenges. The gain comes directly at the expense of review protections for the communities hosting the plants.

industries.industry: Environmental review participants (community groups, conservation organizations)
industries.note: The bill trims the process these groups rely on to see and challenge a project's environmental record, and a 150-day filing deadline would make litigation far harder. They benefit from the bill's failure.

industries.industry: Federal historic and environmental protection programs (NHPA, NEPA administration)
industries.note: The bill carves chip projects out of both NEPA and the National Historic Preservation Act and shifts lead-agency authority to Commerce, weakening the reach of both statutes for this sector while leaving them intact elsewhere.
